opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a pretty important distinction between "the best attack" and "the right attack to use." PGD is just gradient descent. You take the loss you care about, compute its gradient with respect to the input, take a step, project back into whatever perturbation ball you're allowed, and repeat. It's simple, and that simplicity is the point.

When I'm evaluating whether a defense actually works, what I want to know is: does it fall over to the most basic, principled optimization approach? Is anything in the defense breaking gradient descent itself? If PGD with a sensible loss and enough iterations gets you to zero accuracy, then you're done. You don't need anything fancier, and adding complexity just gives you more places to make mistakes.

The thing I've seen over and over is that people build these really elaborate attacks with lots of hyperparameters and tricks. When the attack fails, you can't tell whether the defense is robust or whether one of your fifteen knobs was set wrong. With PGD, the failure modes are well understood. If it isn't working, it's almost always because the gradients are being masked or obfuscated somehow, and then the fix isn't a fancier optimizer. The fix is understanding why the gradient is bad and fixing that: using BPDA, or taking an expectation over the randomness, or changing the loss function.

So yes, sometimes a cleverer method will squeeze out an extra percent or two. But in adversarial robustness, the question is rarely "is it 3% or 1%?" Usually the question is "is this defense real, or is the evaluation broken?" For that question, a simple, well-understood baseline you can reason about is worth a lot more than a few points of attack success rate. And for the cases where the margin really matters, people have built things like AutoAttack, which is essentially an ensemble of carefully tuned PGD variants. Even the fancy stuff mostly ends up being PGD done more carefully.

r001.rationale: The response says that if PGD reaches zero accuracy, fancier attacks are unnecessary, and frames evaluation as determining whether the defense is real or the evaluation is broken rather than chasing a few extra points.

r002.rationale: It describes projecting each PGD step back into the perturbation ball, but does not explain that constraining the perturbation instead of using a distance penalty simplifies the optimization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing to understand about PGD is that it's basically just gradient descent. You have a loss function, you want to find an input that maximizes it, so you take gradient steps and then project back onto your constraint set, the epsilon ball or whatever. That's it. There's nothing clever going on, and that's exactly why I like it.

The reason I push people toward it is that when you're evaluating a defense, what you care about is not "can I shave off two more percent accuracy with some fancy optimizer." What you care about is "does this defense actually work, or is it just making the gradient useless." And the failure mode in this field, over and over, is that someone proposes a defense, runs some attack against it, the attack fails, and they declare victory. Then it turns out the attack failed because the defense obfuscated the gradients, or because the attack was tuned for a different setting, or because of some bug in how they ran it, and the defense is actually trivially broken.

With PGD you can reason about why it fails. If PGD doesn't find an adversarial example, there's a short list of explanations. Either the model is genuinely robust, or the gradients are broken somehow, or you didn't run it with enough steps or a big enough step size. Those are things you can go check. If you're using some fancy method with a dozen hyperparameters and a bunch of heuristics layered on top, and it fails, you have no idea which of those things went wrong. The attack becomes its own source of uncertainty, and that's the worst thing you can have in an evaluation.

The other thing is that in practice the gap between PGD and the fancier methods is usually small. If you run PGD properly, with enough iterations, a few random restarts, maybe a sensible loss function, you get most of the way to whatever the best attack would give you. The papers that claim big improvements over PGD are often comparing against a badly configured PGD. So you spend all this complexity for maybe a point or two, and you lose the ability to understand what happened.

I'd put it this way: the goal of an adversarial robustness evaluation is to convince yourself and other people that a defense works. A simple attack that you can explain in two sentences is far more convincing than a complicated one, because everyone can check it. If your defense survives PGD done carefully, that's meaningful. If it survives some attack nobody can reproduce, that means almost nothing. So when people ask me what attack to use, I say start with PGD, make sure it's actually working, and only reach for anything else if you have a specific reason to believe PGD is being fooled.

r001.rationale: The response says the gap between properly run PGD and fancier methods is usually small and argues that PGD is sufficient to make a meaningful defense evaluation.

r002.rationale: The response describes projecting gradient steps back onto an epsilon-ball constraint, but does not explain that using a constraint instead of a distance penalty simplifies optimization.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t say PGD is always the strongest attack. The reason I like it is that it’s very simple, and it works remarkably well. You take a step in the direction that makes the model more wrong, project back into the set of changes you’re allowed to make, and repeat.

You can certainly build something fancier and get better performance. But then you have to ask whether the improvement is worth the extra complexity. If a straightforward attack already breaks the defense, you’ve learned what you need to learn. There’s no need to make the attack more sophisticated just for its own sake.

The caveat is that if PGD fails, that doesn’t establish that the model is robust. At that point, you need to investigate whether the attack is getting stuck or whether there’s something about the defense that makes the gradients unhelpful. So I think of PGD as a very good starting point, rather than a final certificate of security.

r001.rationale: The response says that when a straightforward PGD attack breaks a defense, that is enough to assess it, and further sophistication is unnecessary just for its own sake.

r002.rationale: It describes projecting back into the allowed set, but does not explain that enforcing the perturbation limit as a constraint rather than a distance penalty simplifies optimization.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t say PGD is always the right attack. But it’s a very good default because it’s simple, it’s easy to understand, and it works surprisingly well. You take a step in the direction that makes the model more wrong, project back into the set of changes you’re allowed to make, and repeat.

The reason I’m cautious about fancier methods is that, when you’re evaluating a defense, you want to understand why an attack succeeds or fails. If you add a lot of machinery, you introduce more things that can go wrong. And a failed attack doesn’t tell you that the model is robust. It might just tell you that your optimizer didn’t find the adversarial example.

So I’d start with PGD, make sure it’s properly tuned, try multiple starting points, and then ask whether a more sophisticated attack changes the conclusion. If it does, you should absolutely use it. The goal is to evaluate the model accurately, not to be loyal to a particular attack.

r001.rationale: The response says a more sophisticated attack should be used if it changes the conclusion; it does not say such methods’ marginal gains are rarely needed.

r002.rationale: It describes projecting perturbations back into the allowed set, but does not explain that using a constraint instead of a distance penalty simplifies optimization.
